headline: Mission Complete — Who Are You Really?
message:
Monday, 1:47 PM. The engagement log had a new section.

--- SERVICE IDENTIFICATION COMPLETE ---

45.77.180.10 — Development Server:
22/tcp   open     OpenSSH 7.4 (protocol 2.0)        — Confirmed via banner + -sV
80/tcp   open     Apache httpd 2.4.49 ((Unix))      — Confirmed via banner + -sV
443/tcp  open     Apache httpd 2.4.49 ((Unix))      — Confirmed via banner + -sV
3306/tcp filtered [version unknown — probe blocked] — Active unknown. Follow-up required.

45.77.180.11 — Legacy Server:
22/tcp   open     OpenSSH 7.4 (protocol 2.0)        — Confirmed via banner + -sV
80/tcp   open     Apache httpd 2.4.49 ((Unix))      — Confirmed via banner + -sV
8443/tcp open     Apache Tomcat 7.0.37              — Confirmed via banner + -sV

Maya looked at the list for a long moment.

'Apache 2.4.49 on both servers,' James said. 'Same version on both. Same Apache on four ports across two different machines.'

'Deployed from the same base image, probably,' Maya said. 'Or the same configuration runbook. Both servers built the same way, at the same time.' She paused. 'Which means a vulnerability in Apache 2.4.49 does not affect one host. It affects both.'

James was looking at port 8443. 'And Tomcat 7.0.37.'

'And Tomcat 7.0.37.' Maya opened a browser. She navigated to nvd.nist.gov and typed: apache tomcat 7.0.37. The results appeared within seconds. James read the severity labels down the list. High. Medium. High. High.

'Is any of that remotely exploitable?' he asked.

'That requires more than reading a CVE title,' she said. 'You need to read the full description, check the affected version range, understand the prerequisites, and determine whether this specific installation meets the conditions.' She switched browser tabs. She had already run the second search. James read the first result on the new tab.

CVE-2021-41773. Apache HTTP Server 2.4.49. Path traversal and remote code execution. CVSS 9.8 in configurations with mod_cgi enabled.

He said nothing for a moment.

'That is on both servers,' he said.

'That is on both servers,' Maya confirmed. She saved the output — all three Nmap formats, both hosts, clearly named. 'Now we know who is home. We know their names and their versions.' She closed the browser. 'The next question is which of them is actually vulnerable — and whether we can prove it.'

She looked at him.

'That is Mission 4.'

---

In this mission, you crossed from 'we know which doors are open' to 'we know who is standing behind each one.'

You learned that a port number is a convention and a service label is a guess — and that professional assessment does not stop at conventions or guesses. Service fingerprinting converts both into confirmed intelligence: specific software, specific version, specific history.

You learned that the version number is not metadata. It is the key that unlocks the CVE database. The difference between 'a web server is running here' and 'Apache httpd 2.4.49 is running here' is the difference between an observation with nowhere to go and a finding that connects directly to CVE-2021-41773, a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability with a publicly available exploit. That specific chain of evidence is what makes a professional assessment findable, reportable, and actionable.

You also learned that banners can be changed — but behaviour cannot. An administrator who removes the Server header has made a cosmetic change to a badge. Nmap -sV reads the accent, not the badge.

The BVR sequence — Banner, Version, Research — is how you approach every open port from here forward. Read the banner. Confirm the version. Search the CVE database with that exact version. The next mission begins at the third step.

Eight services. Eight confirmed versions. One question behind every one of them: which of these is vulnerable?

badgesUnlocked.name: Identity Confirmed
badgesUnlocked.description: Completed Mission 3: Who Are You Really? — built the complete service identity map for the Meridian Financial engagement. Used banner grabbing and Nmap -sV to confirm the software name and version for every open service on both target hosts. Recognised that modified banners do not prevent behavioural fingerprinting, understood why end-of-life software versions require urgent follow-up, and connected version numbers to CVE database research as the foundation for Mission 4.

nextSteps: Mission 4: Which of Them Is Vulnerable? — You have software identities and version numbers. The CVE database is waiting. Mission 4 introduces vulnerability research and validation — systematically connecting confirmed version strings to known CVEs, understanding CVSS scores, and distinguishing theoretical vulnerabilities from confirmed exposures in the target environment.

Optional: Return to the service detection lab and attempt the hidden banner challenge — identify a service that has had its banner modified to claim a different software identity. Confirm the true identity through -sV behavioural fingerprinting and document the discrepancy as you would in an engagement report.
Review: The BVR framework (Banner → Version → Research) is your service identification sequence for every engagement from here forward. Apply it to every open port, in that order, without exception.
